ratings.comment: Clap trigger replaces buttons with an easy action, though accidental triggers and a single default cycle limit its usefulness.
Ambient time display is novel but only adds feedback and doesn't simplify operating the controls.
Reducing to two modes is simple and very feasible, but it is an incremental idea rather than a radical one.
A self-stirring paddle removes the need for user action, but it is mechanically awkward in a microwave and doesn't address the controls.
Door-glass icons guide the user intuitively, though a transparent display that works in a microwave is challenging.
Smell-based done alert is wild and removes symbols, but dispensing scent is impractical, may be unwanted, and doesn't address operation of controls.
Simple and cheap, but fixed power hurts cooking quality for defrosting and delicate foods, and it only partly addresses learning.
One button with additive time is nearly zero learning curve and very cheap, though not very radical.
A mechanical click dial is intuitive and feasible, but similar to existing dial microwaves.
Popcorn buttons are already common, and it covers only a single task.
Replaces the bulb, but interior lighting has almost no bearing on operational learning curve, and a glowing film on a door is awkward near microwave shielding.
Easy door closing helps simplicity, but the safety interlocks can't be replaced by magnets alone and many microwaves already latch by pushing the door shut.
A large press area for opening removes the need to find a button, which is plausible and modestly helpful.
Foot-operated opening is unusual and hands-free, but a low kick plate is awkward on countertop units and adds little to simplicity.
A spoken 'done' is cheap and easy to build and clearly understood, but voice alerts are already common and only cover a small part of operation.
Directly delivers zero-learning operation, but one-touch auto-cook with sensors already exists and is not very radical.
Push-open doors already exist; it simplifies one action but leaves the cooking controls untouched.
A foot pedal is unusual and hands-free, but it adds a new learned element and does not simplify cooking operation.
A transparent casing is impractical because of microwave shielding requirements and barely affects ease of operation.
A camera and screen give a clear view but add cost and complexity, and they are a weak fit for simple operation.
Easy to build and reduces numeric learning, but it only covers power level and is an incremental UI tweak rather than a radical one.
A mechanical twist timer with a visual display is simple and intuitive, but it resembles classic mechanical microwave dials.
A sand timer is intuitive for showing time, but it does not set cooking time or control the oven, and a fixed duration is of limited use.
Stopping automatically on doneness would remove the need to learn anything, but reliable aroma sensing across varied foods is hard.
Acoustic popcorn detection is feasible and already exists in some products, so it is automatic but narrow and only moderately novel.

A projected outline is a fun addition, but it adds a part instead of substituting one, and food placement is not the main learning barrier (setting time and power is), so it serves the need only partly.
It does substitute a component (the turntable), but centering barely affects ease of operation, and a magnetic turntable inside a microwave is questionable given the metal and the heat.
A single weight-sensing button replaces the whole keypad and directly delivers zero-learning operation, though it can't tell food types apart and the mechanism is thinly described.
Gesture control is touch-free but adds an interaction users must learn, so it doesn't clearly simplify operation and may be less intuitive than a button.
App control already exists and adds complexity (pairing, phone required), which works against a no-learning-curve goal.
Scanning food packaging QR codes is simple and feasible, but it depends on codes being present and is only a modest step beyond existing barcode-cook features.
Voice feedback helps guidance but doesn't substitute or simplify the controls, and it's a common existing feature.
A twist timer is a proven, zero-learning-curve control, but it's already common on cheap microwaves and not radical.
Removing the cover is easy but doesn't simplify operation, and it raises safety and RF-shielding concerns for a microwave.
A top-load iris is novel and simplifies loading, but sealing against microwave leakage and spills is hard, and it doesn't address controls.
A conveyor is radical but bulky, with difficult shielding, and it removes little of the real operating complexity.
Zero-setting auto-cook fully removes the learning curve, but it is vague and not very novel, and reliable food recognition is hard.
Directly removes timer adjustment and is simple to use, but similar preset buttons already exist and it is not radical.
A hands-free door is novel, but gesture detection can misfire and it addresses only door opening, not the main operation.
A technically sound part swap, but invisible to the user and does little for the no-learning-curve need.
Easy to build and mildly clearer, but it only affects the end alert, not operation.
A familiar pull-cord start is intuitive and quirky, but a mechanical cord on a microwave is awkward and offers a fixed time only.
A single press-and-turn knob directly delivers no-learning-curve operation and is highly feasible, though similar knob microwaves already exist.
Wave-to-start is simple, but accidental triggering is a risk, an empty or unsafe start is possible, and the default cycle may not suit the food.
Reed switches are a hidden internal change that barely affects user operation, and safety interlocks generally need redundant mechanical reliability.
A fabric RF gasket is a novel substitution, but it has little to do with ease of use and leakage and durability make it questionable.
Bleed resistors are already standard in microwaves and are invisible to the user, so they do little for operational simplicity.
Inverter microwaves already exist and the user-facing benefit for a no-learning-curve interface is indirect.
Solid-state RF is a real emerging technology that enables automatic control, but the link to simple operation depends on an interface that isn't specified.
It's an internal seal change with almost no effect on the user's operation, and gaskets raise wear and leakage concerns.
It's a plausible, easy swap that removes a minor maintenance task, but it doesn't make operation simpler and isn't radical.
Wireless power for a high-draw appliance is inefficient and impractical, and it solves a non-problem since plugging in is already easy.
Camera-based doneness detection would remove all settings and directly serve zero-learning operation, though it is technically hard in a microwave and is not really a cheaper substitution.
Phone NFC tap is feasible and concrete, but it needs a phone and an app, which adds a learning step and is not very radical.
Wave-to-open is simple and intuitive, but it only covers opening the door, not the cooking operation.
An EL panel for interior light barely touches operation simplicity, since lighting is already automatic in microwaves.
A transparent heater film is radical and simplifies the structure, but it does little for ease of use and is doubtful as a microwave heating method.
Popcorn buttons already exist on most microwaves, so this is neither radical nor new, though it is simple and works.
Beverage presets are already common and only modestly simplify operation, with little radical thinking.
Frozen-meal presets exist, but auto two-stage cooking helps; package variability limits reliability.
Adds a safety gesture rather than simplifying operation, so it only weakly serves the no-learning-curve need.
A radical no-controls microwave maximizes simplicity, but reliable food detection and cook-time inference are hard, and the mechanism is vague.
Removing the power knob simplifies things, but users still need to set time, and temperature feedback in a microwave is technically hard.
A single time slider with automatic power is simple and easy to build, though it is an incremental change.
One button that cycles through food presets and starts is very simple, though cycling and the timing of the start are slightly ambiguous.
A pictogram dial with detents and push-to-start is intuitive, cheap, and mechanically proven.
Large color-coded buttons are easy to recognize and cheap to make, but they are a common, obvious approach.
Familiar twist timer is easy to use, but microwaves have long used mechanical dials, so it is hardly radical.
A sand timer that trips the power is quirky and intuitive, though timing accuracy and the safety switch are problematic.
One-button reheat with a humidity sensor is highly simple and feasible, but sensor cooking already exists on the market.
Camera food recognition removes all input, but it is costly and not a cheaper substitute, and recognition errors are likely.
Press start and it stops at 60 C, which is simple, but surface-only IR readings give uneven results.
Weight-derived automatic timing removes the main decision, though weight alone poorly predicts heating needs for different foods.
Simple and feasible, but it only modestly simplifies and still leaves the time decision.
A single-button cycle collapses controls, but it's ambiguous without a base time and may confuse users about what 'more' means.
Proximity-activated opening is feasible but addresses door opening, not the core cooking operation, and risks accidental opening.
A sliding door is intuitive but hard to seal against microwave leakage and has little effect on cooking operation.
Container-embedded RFID automates programming and is fairly novel, though it needs special tagged containers and RFID tags must be microwave-safe.
Weight-based auto power is plausible and simplifies things, but weight alone doesn't tell cook time or food type, and similar sensors already exist.
Humidity sensing for auto-stop removes the timer and is feasible, but it is already common in sensor-cook microwaves.
Steam detection is a proven approach that removes timer entry, but it is nearly identical to the humidity idea and not very radical.
Acoustic popcorn detection is clever and feasible, but it is limited to popcorn so it serves the simplicity need narrowly.
Flat-floor microwaves with stirrers already exist and are easy to use, but they have little effect on operating complexity.
Relying on ambient light is unreliable, especially in a dark kitchen, and it barely helps usability.
Automatic door lighting is already standard, and it adds little to the target need.
A push-to-open, self-closing magnetic door is a plausible convenience, but it only touches door handling and not operating the controls.
The safety interlock is hidden from the user and does nothing to remove the learning curve.
A clear window does little for operation simplicity, and ITO at microwave-blocking thickness and durability is questionable, though it is a concrete substitution.
Mode stirrers already exist and removing the turntable does cut a part, but the gain in learning-curve terms is modest.
A flat tray without rotation gives uneven heating and barely affects operation simplicity.
It is essentially the same as the mode stirrer idea, a feasible and common approach that removes a user-managed part.
An automatic door pop on completion removes a step and is a plausible, concrete mechanism that suits a no-learning-curve goal.
Light-switch style heating is simple but needs auto-safe stop and risks overheating or forgotten food, with a vague mechanism.
Removing power choice is easy and simplifying, but a single fixed power gives poor results for many foods.
A mechanical spring timer with a single twist is intuitive, cheap and proven, though the five-minute limit is restrictive.
One big start button is very easy to use but is a familiar approach and the default cycle may not suit all foods.
A magnetic catch removes a control, but opening the door still needs a mechanism, and the benefit to operation is marginal.
Plate-embedded RFID presets remove settings, but it requires proprietary plates and doesn't cover arbitrary dishes.
A thermal camera for auto-stop removes timer input and is plausible, since low-res IR sensors are cheap and already appear in some ovens.
Packaging-based indicators are clever but need a new bag ecosystem and reliable sensing in a microwave field.
Steam-sensing closed-loop power is workable and removes the power knob, but it doesn't remove time or start decisions.
A single any-position dial is very simple and easy to build, but it's a modest idea rather than a radical one and offers limited control.
Easy to build, but it addresses cleaning rather than operation learning curve, and liners already exist in similar forms.
Wireless power at microwave-level wattage is difficult and inefficient, and plugging in is not a real learning barrier.
Solid-state RF is real and enables precise automatic cooking, which supports one-button use, though cost remains high.
A static metamaterial lens for even heating is interesting but hard to make work across varied loads, and it only indirectly helps usability.
Acoustic levitation stirring of food is very radical but physically implausible at this scale and in this environment, and its link to simple operation is weak.
Tag-based auto-programming eliminates the interface entirely, but requires packaged food ecosystem adoption and doesn't suit arbitrary foods.
A single-twist mechanical timer is very simple and cheap, though such dial timers already exist and it offers limited control.
A spoken 'done' is easy to build but only marginally helps operation simplicity and is a minor substitution.
Mode stirrers are already standard in many microwaves and only loosely address learning-curve simplicity.
A magnetic stirring bowl removes a manual step, but a metal stirrer in a microwave is technically problematic and it's a niche accessory.
Microwave doors already use perforated mesh that lets you see in, so this is barely new and does little for operation simplicity.
A transparent OLED status display on the door is novel and eases reading status, but it does not simplify controlling the oven.
An EL panel replaces the bulb, but this has almost no effect on ease of operation and the panel would struggle in a hot, RF-heavy cavity.
LED lighting is an obvious, cheap substitution with little bearing on learning curve.
Mode stirrers are common in existing microwaves and remove the turntable hassle, which modestly helps simplicity.
Visual and intuitive, but a rotating hourglass is an awkward way to set a cook time, and it adds little over a simple dial.
A mechanical sand timer is a charming substitute for the electronic timer, but fixed intervals and unreliable accuracy limit it.

Opening the door already stops microwaves in standard designs, so this is not new and only slightly reduces the learning burden.

Easy to build and intuitive, but picture labels are a modest, familiar change rather than a radical one.

Clear labels and three choices make it intuitive, though it resembles existing preset panels.

Easy to build but only addresses end-of-cycle notification, not operation, and voice prompts are already common; it is not a substitution or radical.
Intuitive display substitution that helps at a glance, but it only affects feedback, not setting up the cook, and is modest in novelty.

IR temperature-based stop is plausible and removes guessing, though surface-only readings limit accuracy and it is not very wild.
A simple dial is easy and familiar, but unnumbered clicks make results ambiguous and it is not radical.
Wave-to-start is simple but a default cycle fits few foods and risks accidental starts.
A foot pedal door only addresses opening, not operating or learning the controls, so it barely serves the need.
Removing the power knob simplifies things and is plausible, but time and start controls still remain, so the learning curve is only partly removed.
Color-coded buttons are easy to build, but mapping colors to food types is arbitrary and not very radical.
A picture dial is intuitive and easy to make, though similar presets already exist and portion size is not handled.
Touching anywhere on the door to start is novel and simple, but the default cooking could be wrong and could start by accident, which is unsafe on an empty cavity.
Removing every control and cooking automatically on door close is radical and fully removes the learning curve, but sensor cooking accuracy and the lack of any override are real limits.
A one-button leftover mode is simple to use, but it is a standard preset, and mixed meals make a safe default vague.
Frozen-meal buttons already exist on most microwaves, so this is easy to build but barely new and not radical.
Beverage buttons are already common and easy to use, with little innovation and no real substitution of parts.
The popcorn button is ubiquitous and understood by everyone, but it is the opposite of a wild idea.
A potato preset is already standard and covers a narrow use case, so it adds little to the need.
Voice control removes the panel entirely and is plausible, but it is a known concept and can struggle with noise and accents.
Scanning the package is a concrete mechanism that removes manual entry, though it depends on barcode and instruction databases, and not every package would work.
One-press cooking until done is the ideal for no learning curve, but reliable doneness sensing across foods is technically hard.
A dial is simple, but it still needs the user to learn how it behaves, and microwaves cannot easily regulate to a target temperature without sensing.
Very easy to build and use, but it already exists on most microwaves and covers only one task.
Highly relevant and easy to build, but one-touch start buttons already exist and it is not radical or a real substitution.
Auto-sensing removes decisions and is plausible, but humidity sensor cooking exists and the mechanism is vague.
Voice control exists in commercial microwaves, and it adds complexity and failure modes rather than removing a learning curve.
Opening the door by gesture does little for operation simplicity and could be unreliable or accidental.
The idea is concrete and a substitution, but it barely serves ease of operation and is largely redundant since mesh doors already exist.
Bleeder resistors already exist in microwaves and have nothing to do with ease of operation, so it is neither radical nor relevant.
Thermal fuses and PTC resets are standard, and the user rarely meets a reset step anyway, so it barely helps the learning curve.
Automatic metal detection removes a rule users would otherwise have to learn, though reliable sensing in a cavity is hard and it isn't a substitution.
Pulsed heating that prevents superheating without user knowledge is plausible and useful, but it targets a narrow case and the steam-burst mechanism is vague.
A lid or stick sensor with an icon is feasible, but it adds a warning the user must understand and falls short of zero learning.
Pizza-specific auto cycle is useful, but it is a narrow food category and does not clearly substitute a part with something simpler.
Sensor-based vegetable steaming removes timing knowledge, but it is a category-specific button that existing sensor-cook microwaves already approximate.

ratings.feasibility_note: probe-free thickness and core temperature sensing is hard
ratings.comment: Safety benefit is real, but detecting meat thickness and starting temperature without a probe is technically doubtful.
Gentle fish cycle is sensible, yet it is highly similar to the other ideas and very niche.
Rice reheating via weight and humidity sensing is quite feasible, but it is incremental and a narrow use case.
Photoluminescent liner is plausible and replaces the bulb, but glow fades and it barely affects operational simplicity.
Light pipe is clever, but it can't leak microwaves, depends on room light, and doesn't simplify operation much.
Stationary mode stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves and genuinely remove the turntable, so it is feasible but not radical.
A plate spinning from cavity airflow with no motor is physically dubious, and the 'magnetic' mechanism is unclear.
A disposable paper plate on a fixed support is plausible, but it creates waste and has limited effect on learning curve.
